clue.text: Is solving this clue depressing?

definitions.meaning: solving a Down clue in a crossword is entering one Down answer
something that dispirits you is wearing you out and lowering your mood

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is itself a Down clue, so solving it literally means securing one Down entry; the second sense is the idiom for being dispiriting.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means making someone feel low, and literally describes filling in a Down light.

clue.text: What's on extraterrestrial map?

indicators.note: in a Down clue, one piece placed on another comes after it, below it in the grid

parts.note: a map is a plan or chart
ET is the abbreviation for extraterrestrial, as in the film alien

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what would be marked on an alien's chart.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a world is exactly what a map of space beyond Earth would show.
explanation.definitionFit: A world such as Mars is the kind of feature that appears on a chart of outer space.

clue.text: There's nothing more apt, with Rome so corrupted

definitions.text: There's nothing more apt, with Rome so corrupted

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

indicators.note: corrupted signals that the letters of the fodder are spoilt and put into a new order

explanation.surface: A comment that no phrase better suits a decadent Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Cicero's Latin cry 'Oh the times! Oh the customs!' lamented Roman corruption, so the whole clue also describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero's Latin exclamation laments the decline of morals in his day, apt for a decadent Rome.

clue.text: Post back Elvis Number Ten — nut reorders remix

indicators.note: a remix rearranges a recording, here the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: A music-press note about an Elvis track and a Number Ten remix.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition has two senses: the Post Office endorsement on undeliverable mail, and a 1962 Elvis Presley hit. 'Number Ten' looks like Downing Street, but only TEN is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Undeliverable mail is marked with this phrase for the postman to take back, and it is also the title of an Elvis Presley song.

clue.text: Affected player, or a match, badly

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sportsman putting on airs, or a game played poorly.
explanation.definitionFit: An overacting performer who hams it up is an affected stage player.

clue.text: Old stone implements decomposed in the soil

indicators.note: decomposed means broken down, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ancient tools rotting away underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaeologists use this term for crude flints from the dawn of the Stone Age.

clue.text: Having UN seats, so a Thai represented this part of the world?

definitions.text: Having UN seats, so a Thai represented this part of the world?

indicators.note: represented read as re-presented means presented again in a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A Thai diplomat speaking for a region at the United Nations.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a Thai delegate at the UN would be speaking for this region, which includes Thailand.
explanation.definitionFit: Thailand lies in the region east of India and south of China, so a Thai is from that part of the world.

clue.text: Cry by Conservative in frantic -e-mail

indicators.note: in places the first pieces within the anagrammed letters
frantic means wild and agitated, so the letters of the word after it are scrambled

parts.note: by as in 'two by three' is the multiplication sign X

explanation.surface: A shout from a Tory politician in an agitated electronic message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frantic' turns EMAIL into ELAIM; X and C go between its first letter and the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclaim is to call out suddenly, a synonym for crying out.

clue.text: Book to fool both teams?

parts.note: to catch someone out is to trick or fool them
two sides of eleven players, as in football or cricket, make twenty-two

explanation.surface: A trick to deceive both sides in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Heller's novel gives the book; football and cricket teams have eleven players each.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Heller's 1961 novel is a famous work of fiction, hence a book.

clue.text: Very cross about gran going to Kent for play

indicators.note: going to means joined onto, so the following piece is added at the end
about means surrounding, so the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: nan is an informal word for grandmother, like gran
Clark Kent is the alter ego of the comic-book hero

explanation.surface: A furious reaction to a grandmother travelling to the English county of Kent for a theatre trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent looks like the English county, but it is Clark Kent, the mild reporter identity of the comic-book hero; the play is by George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw wrote this drama in 1903, a well-known stage work.

clue.text: See 25
American flier's instantly admitted to union

indicators.note: admitted to means let inside, so the second piece sits within the first

parts.note: TU is the abbreviation for trade union
'in a mo' is informal for in a moment, instantly

explanation.surface: A US airman promptly signing up to a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flier' suggests a pilot, but it is a bird: a ground-dwelling bird of Central and South America.
explanation.definitionFit: This partridge-like bird lives in Central and South America and can fly, so it is an American flying creature.

clue.text: Put out, getting wet transportation to London

indicators.note: out means not in its usual state, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: the wet means rainy weather, rain

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed at being soaked on the way into the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as annoyed, but 'out' rearranges PUT to give UPT. In British railway usage an up-train runs towards London.
explanation.definitionFit: On British railways a service heading to the capital is called the up-train, so it is a train bound for London.

clue.text: Less incorrect

definitions.meaning: as in '... much', meaning to a smaller degree
a reply that says something is untrue or wrong

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase can mean to a smaller degree, and is also a retort denying a claim is true.

clue.text: Term of endearment repeatedly used in Athens of the North

indicators.note: used in means the letters are found inside the words; repeatedly because they appear inside two separate runs of them

explanation.surface: A pet name heard often in Edinburgh, called the Athens of the North.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run inside 'atHENs' and again across 'tHE North'. Edinburgh is nicknamed the Athens of the North, and Scots there call women 'hen' as an affectionate address.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland and northern England women are addressed affectionately as 'hen', like 'dear' or 'love'.

clue.text: Discover success, nothing new

parts.note: a hit is a success, as in a hit record
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Finding a winner without anything novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To come upon an idea by chance is to discover or stumble on it.

clue.text: Create problem or solve one for later birds?

definitions.meaning: to start trouble that is hard to contain
the early bird catches the worm; latecomers are helped if the worm tin is unsealed for them

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the early bird catches the worm' is behind the second sense: late risers would need their worms supplied ready in an unsealed tin.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means stirring up a complicated mess; literally, unsealing a tin of bait would solve the late birds' food problem.

clue.text: Crazy spell of wackiest witches here?

indicators.note: crazy spell suggests the letters of the following word are spelt out in a mad order

explanation.surface: A mad incantation from the zaniest coven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell' here is the spelling of the letters, not a witch's charm. John Updike's novel The Witches of Eastwick is set in a fictional New England town.
explanation.definitionFit: John Updike's novel The Witches of Eastwick names this town as the coven's home.

clue.text: Where one might see race records set by old master

parts.note: OM is short for old master, a great painter of the past

explanation.surface: A racegoer's note on records set by an old champion.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom Downs in Surrey stages the Derby, England's most famous flat horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs, a Surrey racecourse, hosts the Derby, so it is a place to watch horses running.

clue.text: One of a group of digits three's first .. two, one, finally

definitions.text: One of a group of digits

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the word before it is taken
finally means the closing letter of each of the two words before it is taken

explanation.surface: A countdown reading three, two, one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digits' suggests numbers, which the countdown backs up, but the digits are on the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Digits are fingers and toes, and the foot has five of the latter.

clue.text: A call made by court official in bed

definitions.text: A call made by court official
definitions.meaning: the umpire's cry when a ball has bounced twice before being returned, in tennis or squash
someone still lying down has not risen yet

explanation.walkthrough: 'court' looks legal, but it is a tennis or squash court, whose umpire calls a ball that has bounced twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket-sports umpire calls a double bounce with this phrase, and someone lying in bed has not risen.

clue.text: Very powerful person protecting one great artist

indicators.note: protecting means shielding all round, so the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: a titan is a person of great power or importance
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A mighty figure shielding a lone painter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian Renaissance master Tiziano Vecellio is one of the greatest painters.

clue.text: Where sisters are seen in continuation

definitions.meaning: senior nurses in British hospitals are called sisters and work in hospital rooms for patients
carrying on forward from a point

explanation.walkthrough: In a British hospital a sister is a senior nurse, found on the wards.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it places nurses in hospital; as one, it means forward from now on.

clue.text: Doris as celebrity in The Sun?

parts.note: Doris Day was the American singer and film actress

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about Doris Day as a celebrity in The Sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Sun' looks like the British tabloid newspaper, but it is the sun in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Daystar is a poetic name for the sun, the star that brings daylight.

clue.text: Ignore diamonds on display

explanation.surface: Overlooking diamonds put on show.
explanation.walkthrough: To freeze someone out is to snub them; this phrase means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclude or cold-shoulder someone is to snub them, as with freezing out.

clue.text: Where many Cypriots live is in a resort accommodating small business

indicators.note: accommodating means taking in, so the second piece goes inside the first
resort read as re-sort means sort again, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: A seaside town with a little firm in it, home to many islanders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town, but as re-sort it rearranges IS IN A into NISIA; CO goes after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Cyprus is home to a large share of the island's population.

clue.text: A little fighting over experimental figures

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the whole run of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: a tad is a little bit

explanation.surface: A small skirmish over results from a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns the whole run A, TAD, WAR backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Unprocessed measurements from an experiment are unanalysed numbers.
